This has already been mostly answered by others, but I'll throw in my explanation. In Latin the letters U and V are sort of the same, but sort of not. Originally there was only V, which was a vowel that sometimes functioned like a consonant. Often when it preceded another vowel it functioned similar to our letter W. When both V and U are used, V is generally the consonantal function of the vowel, and U is the regular vowel sound like oo in boot. I think U developed initially as part of lower case letters which developed as sort of cursive variants of the original Latin letters which originally didn't have lower case letters. Cursive probably isn't actually the right word, but it's close because there's actually a whole lot more to how lower case letters developed than can be expressed by a single word. That's not the whole history of the letter, there's also the English side of the history, but I don't know that well enough to BS it offhand. Nowadays I'd expect most classical Latinists to mostly only use V when writing in all caps and only use U when writing in all lower case or in mixed case, unless they're writing for beginners, then I'd expect them to sometimes be used together. That's not to say that all texts that mix them are for beginners. I'd expect ecclesiastical Latinists to usually use both letters regardless of the letter case used. Both types of Latinists read stuff from one another and have their own preferences, so it's not at all a hard and fast rule. But V in Ecclesiastical Latin either usually or always makes a V sound like in English and has more of a connection to Italian and that connection with Italian as well as their connection to later Latin is why they're more likely to use both. Sometimes classical purists will write in all caps and without punctuation, but that's a pain in the ass to read. It would be interesting to see whether somebody could be raised to prefer it be written like that all the time. Good classical Latin essentially has the punctuation built into the language, but most people who learn the language nowadays aren't good at consistently speaking like that. For example: You understand? versus DOYOUUNDERSTAND because YOUUNDERSTAND without a question mark is a statement, not a question.

Edit: Also short paragraphs and sentences make for easier reading, but sometimes I can't be bothered.
